topic: JVM Internals (Memory Model, G1/ZGC, Class Loading)

questions.question: What is the primary cause of this memory leak in Metaspace?
options: A) Creating a new `GroovyClassLoader` per invocation caches generated class definitions in its internal registry, preventing the `Class` instances and their Metaspace metadata from being garbage collected.
B) The `newInstance()` reflective call allocates object memory in Metaspace instead of the JVM Young Generation heap.
C) The Spring `@Service` singleton proxy holds a strong reference to all local method variables inside `executeRule` across execution threads.
D) Metaspace GC is disabled by default in Java 17 when running with the G1 Garbage Collector unless `-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions` is set.
questions.correct_answer_text: A) Creating a new `GroovyClassLoader` per invocation caches generated class definitions in its internal registry, preventing the `Class` instances and their Metaspace metadata from being garbage collected.
questions.explanation: In the Java Memory Model, Metaspace stores class metadata. A `Class` object can only be unloaded from Metaspace if its defining `ClassLoader` is no longer reachable and eligible for Garbage Collection. By default, `GroovyClassLoader` caches parsed classes in an internal class map. When a new `GroovyClassLoader` is instantiated per request without clearing its cache or properly managing classloader lifecycle, strong references to class objects persist. As a result, the JVM cannot unload these dynamically generated classes during GC, leading to continuous Metaspace growth and an eventual `OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace`.

questions.scenario: You are debugging a production issue where an ultra-low-latency financial processing engine on JDK 17 was migrated from G1 GC to ZGC (`-XX:+UseZGC`). Under high peak volume, application threads encounter sudden latency spikes exceeding 500ms. GC logs reveal concurrent marking/relocation phases operating normally, but show repeated `allocation stall` warnings. Total heap utilization remains under 65% of the maximum heap limit (`-Xmx32g`).
questions.question: What is the primary cause of these latency spikes under ZGC?
options: A) ZGC triggers a Stop-The-World (STW) Full GC phase whenever heap utilization crosses 60% in high-concurrency environments.
B) The application's object allocation rate exceeded the rate at which ZGC could reclaim memory, forcing application threads to stall until space was freed.
C) The ZGC Load Barrier fails on 64-bit architectures when Metaspace is configured without explicit `-XX:MetaspaceSize` bounds.
D) ZGC Colored Pointers cause memory cache line invalidation stalls when GC concurrent thread count exceeds physical CPU cores.
questions.correct_answer_text: B) The application's object allocation rate exceeded the rate at which ZGC could reclaim memory, forcing application threads to stall until space was freed.
questions.explanation: ZGC is a concurrent, low-latency garbage collector that performs most work (marking, relocation, reference processing) in parallel with application threads, achieving sub-millisecond pause times. However, if the application's object allocation rate spikes faster than ZGC's concurrent collection speed, available heap space becomes exhausted before the collection cycle completes. When this occurs, ZGC enforces an 'Allocation Stall', pausing allocation requests in application threads until memory reclamation catches up. Solutions include tuning `-XX:ConcGCThreads`, adjusting `-XX:ZAllocationSpikeTolerance`, or pre-allocating heap room to buffer allocation spikes.

questions.question: What is the primary Java Memory Model (JMM) mechanism causing worker threads to read stale or uninitialized state?
options: A) Non-volatile field assignment allows compiler and CPU instruction reordering and thread-local caching, failing to establish a happens-before relationship between reference assignment and map contents publication.
B) Spring CGLIB proxies generate thread-local copies of `@Component` instance fields, causing cross-thread updates to be ignored.
C) The `HashMap` read operation triggers a write barrier during G1 GC concurrent marking, locking the object reference.
D) Standard `HashMap` operations force safe-point synchronization that suspends reader threads until a full GC cycle runs.
questions.correct_answer_text: A) Non-volatile field assignment allows compiler and CPU instruction reordering and thread-local caching, failing to establish a happens-before relationship between reference assignment and map contents publication.
questions.explanation: Under the Java Memory Model (JMM), updates to standard (non-volatile) fields do not guarantee a 'happens-before' edge across threads. Without `volatile` or explicit synchronization, two critical issues arise: 1) Visibility: worker threads can read stale, CPU-cached values of `configMap` rather than main memory. 2) Reordering: The compiler or CPU can reorder instructions such that the reference `this.configMap = tempMap` becomes visible to other threads *before* `tempMap`'s internal structure and entries are fully published and flushed to memory. Declaring `private volatile Map<String, String> configMap` or using `AtomicReference<Map<String, String>>` ensures strict happens-before ordering and safe publication.
